craft_claim: Noir and hard-boiled registers achieve bleakness through understatement and withheld judgement; where the prose supplies the grief or outrage the reader should produce, the grim tone collapses into melodrama.

supporting_evidence.location: The Dark Side of the Screen, chapters on noir fatalism and style
supporting_evidence.note: Hirsch's critical account of film noir identifies fatalism, moral fog, and understated, hard-boiled delivery as the register's signature; bleakness is atmospheric and ironic rather than declaimed.

Gardner defines sentimentality as demanding an emotional response greater than the situation justifies—the exact failure into which a grim voice falls when it editorialises the sorrow it should let the reader feel.

supporting_evidence.location: Whole novel; pursuit and sheriff passages
supporting_evidence.note: Menace is built through procedural detail and small-talk that defers the threat; violence arrives without editorialising, and the sheriff's dread is carried by memory and weariness.

counterevidence.note: Section C codifies understatement as film noir's inherited genre signature rather than a grim universal, and card section 7 declares high rhetorical lament and Victorian melodrama to be codes where the performance of grief is the point, so supplying the grief collapses the tone only outside such declared codes.

scope: Crime, thriller, and literary prose in a bleak register.
exceptions: Camp, pastiche, or deliberate Victorian melodrama where exaggerated performance is the acknowledged code.
